skill.name: ffind
skill.description: Advanced file finder for firmware analysis, file type detection, and optional embedded filesystem extraction.
skill.summary: Finds firmware file types and guides optional filesystem extraction for IoT security analysis.
skill.author: BrownFineSecurity

security_audit.summary: Most Ruby backtick findings are false positives caused by Markdown inline code and fenced examples. The sudo guidance and temporary extraction paths are confirmed risks because the skill directs privileged filesystem extraction on untrusted firmware inputs. No prompt injection or data exfiltration intent was found.

remediation.issue: Privileged filesystem extraction is shown as a normal workflow.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user approval before sudo, prefer sandboxed execution, and document that firmware inputs are untrusted.

remediation.issue: Extraction output may be written under shared temporary paths.
remediation.suggestion: Use a dedicated user-selected directory with restrictive permissions and avoid predictable names in shared temporary storage.

remediation.issue: External binary and dependency provenance is assumed.
remediation.suggestion: Tell users to verify the ffind binary path and installed filesystem tools before running analysis.

content.value_statement: Firmware images often hide filesystems and security artifacts that are hard to inspect manually. This skill guides ffind analysis to identify file types and plan controlled extraction.
actual_capabilities: Identifies file types across one or more files or directories.
Highlights security-relevant artifact types by default.
Can request all detected file types for broader inventory work.
Supports optional extraction of ext2, ext3, ext4, and F2FS filesystems.
Supports text, quiet, and machine-readable output modes.
limitations: Requires the ffind binary and supporting filesystem tools to be installed.
Filesystem extraction can require administrator privileges.
It does not prove that a firmware image is safe to process.
Results depend on readable input paths and local permissions.

use_cases.title: Inventory Firmware Images
use_cases.description: Identify embedded filesystems, archives, certificates, and scripts before deeper reverse engineering.

use_cases.title: Compare Build Artifacts
use_cases.description: Check whether firmware builds contain expected file types and extractable partitions.

use_cases.title: Triage Unknown Device Data
use_cases.description: Quickly summarize file types in unknown images during an investigation.

prompt_templates.title: Identify File Types
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner analysis of one firmware image.
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze this firmware image with ffind and summarize the detected file types: <path>.

prompt_templates.title: Show Complete Inventory
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate inventory with all detected types.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use ffind to inspect <path> and include common file types, not only security artifacts.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Safe Extraction
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate extraction planning before privileged commands.
prompt_templates.prompt: Check whether <path> contains extractable filesystems. Ask before using elevated privileges or writing output files.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Multiple Images
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced comparison across several firmware files.
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze these firmware images with ffind, compare detected artifact types, and call out extraction candidates: <paths>.

output_examples.input: Analyze a firmware image and summarize artifact types.
output_examples.output: The result lists detected file categories, counts, notable paths, and any filesystems that appear extractable.

output_examples.input: Inspect two firmware files and compare findings.
output_examples.output: The response highlights file types present in both images, types unique to each image, and likely extraction targets.
The response asks for approval before elevated commands and recommends a dedicated output directory with restricted permissions.

best_practices: Confirm target paths before running analysis.
Use a dedicated extraction directory with restrictive permissions.
Treat firmware files as untrusted and avoid unnecessary privileged extraction.
anti_patterns: Running extraction with elevated privileges before the user approves it.
Writing extraction output into shared temporary paths without reviewing permissions.
Assuming missing detections prove that no embedded filesystem exists.

faq.question: What does this skill help analyze?
faq.answer: It helps analyze firmware files, directories, and embedded filesystems with the ffind command.

faq.question: Does it extract filesystems automatically?
faq.answer: No. It guides extraction only when requested, and privileged extraction should require user approval.

faq.question: Which filesystems are mentioned?
faq.answer: The skill mentions ext2, ext3, ext4, and F2FS extraction support.

faq.question: Can it show every file type?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill includes an option to show all detected types, including common formats.

faq.question: What tools must be installed?
faq.answer: The ffind command is required. Extraction also depends on e2fsprogs, f2fs-tools, and util-linux.

faq.question: What is the main safety concern?
faq.answer: The main concern is privileged extraction of untrusted firmware and writing extracted data to temporary paths.
